articles.body_raw:
Abhinaya Harigovind
New Delhi, November 16

IN SEPTEMBER, Sorbonne University, located in Paris,
announced its withdrawal from the ranking produced by
Times Higher Education (THE), becoming yet another
major institution to flag concerns about international
higher education rankings.
Widely publicised and closely watched, global higher
education rankings produced by different organisations,
analysts or platforms, can determine perceptions among
prospective students and employers, and drive policy
decisions. The rankings have, however, drawn flak over
the years. Key concerns among institutions, including
some Indian ones, have been that the rankingsare not
fully transparent in terms of the datathey consider, and
that ascore and rank do not capture the extent and diver-
sity of activities, contributions, and research.
How international rankings work
There are three prominent global higher education
rankings: the QS rankings produced by London-based
Quacquarelli Symonds; the THE rankings, produced by
THE magazine, also headquartered in London; and rank-
ings produced by the ShanghaiRanking Consultancy.
For THE, institutions submit data used for the rank-
ings, which allows them to stop participating in the pro-
cess by withholding these submissions. In contrast, QS
and ShanghaiRanking use public data.

Sorbonne University’s concerns
The institution — ranked 72 in the 2026 QS ranking,
76 in the 2026 THE ranking, and 43 in the 2025 Shanghai
Ranking — flagged concerns about indicators that
measure reputation and research.
“Their (global rankings’) methodology, which focuses
on English-language journals, favours certain
disciplines, while the humanities and social sciences...
are put at a disadvantage... Certain rankings are based on
reputational surveys, which raise numerous concerns,
including scientific, methodological, and ethical issues,”
Sorbonne University told The Indian Express.

The hurdles in India’s
fight to eliminate TB

articles.body_raw:
AnonnaDutt
New Delhi, November 16

WHILE THE burden of tuberculosis in
India continues to decline, the country is
nowhere close toachieving elimination, ac-
cording to the Global TB Report 2025, re-
leased last week.
In2024, India recorded around271lakh
TB cases and more than 3 lakh deaths, the
highest in the world, the World Health Or-
ganization (WHO) analysis said. That said,
India was among the eight high-burden
countries that were able to diagnose more
than 80% of the estimated cases last year.
The findings oftheGlobal TB Reportare
crucial since the Union Health Ministry is
yet to release the India TB report for last
year. Last year, TB was the deadliest infec-
tious killer globally, infecting 107 million
and killing 1.23 million people worldwide.
Reaching elimination targets
In 2018, Prime Minister Narendra Modi
announced India’s ambitious target of
eliminating TB by 2025, five years ahead of
the global target. Although there has been
a consistent decline in the estimated
number of TB cases, as well as the rate of
TB cases per 100,000 population, as 2025
draws to aclose, India is far from its target
of eliminating the bacterial disease.
Note that while elimination is defined
as less than one case per million popula-
tion, the WHO’s “End TB” strategy targets
an easier 80% decline in new TB cases and
90% decline in TB deaths by 2030 (com-
pared with the 2015 baseline).
The Global TB Report 2025 shows that
India has achieved only a21% reductionin
new cases, and a 28% reduction in deaths
between 2015 and 2024. This does not even
come close to the End TB milestones for
2025 — a50% reduction in TB incidence
and 75% reduction in TB deaths. In fact, it
essentially means that India in 2024 was
able to meet only half of the global mile-
stones set for 2020.
Nonetheless, this reduction achieved by
India is still ahead of the global average.
Globally, TBincidence reduced only by 12%
between 2015 and 2024.
DrS KKabra, former professor of paedi-
atric pulmonology at AIIMS, New Delhi,
said: “There is a need to introspect and see
whether the targets were realistic. If they
were, there is aneed to take alook at where
we stand and what the reasons are for us
not reaching the targets. There has to be a
program to consult all stakeholders, such
as the patients, their family members, the
labs, DOT (Directly Observed Treatment
Short Course) centres, doctors, nurses,
regulators, everybody, to look for gaps and
address them.”

fore they develop unfavourabie outcomes,”

Growing at home not allowed
Ifcannabis leavesarenot covered by the
NDPS Act, why can one not grow aplant to

This is where last week’s Kerala HC
order becomes significant.

arately and expiicitiy prohibits the cultiva-
tion of any plant of the genus cannabis.

articles.body_raw:
Vineet Bhalla,
New Delhi, November 16

THE KERALA High Court earlier this
month dismissed a petition bya man seek-
ing to quash proceedings against him for
growing cannabis.
The petitioner had been caught by ex-
cise officials with five cannabis plants in
pots on the terrace of a rented house. His
defence? The plantshad not yet developed
“flowering or fruiting tops”, andthat under
law, only the flowering tops constitute
“ganja”, the drug. The Bench of Justice CS
Dias rejected this argument.
What the NDPS Act says
In 1985, India enacted the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Substances
(NDPS) Act. The law did not impose a blan-
ket ban onevery part of the cannabis plant
Section 2(iii) of the NDPS Act defines
“cannabis (hemp)” to mean both charas,

excludes “the seeds and leaves [of the plant]
when not accompanied by the tops”.
The bhaang loophole

This exclusion of leaves and seeds cre-
ates the legal space for bhaang, the edible
preparation made from the leaves of the
cannabis plant.
Because the NDPS Act does not classify
leaves as “cannabis”, bhaang does not fall
under the definition ofa “narcotic drug”.
But this does not mean bhaang is unregu-
lated. The National Policy on NDPS cla-
rifies that bhaang is subject to state laws.
The Actallowsstate governments topermit
and regulate the cultivation of cannabis
plants and the production, possession, con-
sumption and transport for industrial pur-
poses or for obtaining fibre and seeds.
States like Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan
license authorised dealers to sell bhaang,
while others, such as Assam, have banned
it entirely.

articles.headline_raw: Behind Indigenous people’s demands at COP
articles.body_raw:
AROUND 100 people from Brazil’s
Munduruku Indigenous groupstaged
a protest at the ongoing COP30
climate summit in Belém on Friday,
primarily against the Brazi-
lian government’s plans to {cL
build infrastructure in the
Amazon rainforest. The Munduruku
Ipereg Ayu Movement said in astate-
ment addressing President Lula da
Silva, “Our forest is not forsale. We are
the ones who protect the climate, and
the Amazon cannot continue to be de-

stroyed to enrich large corporations.”
The Brazilian government is in the
process of building a highway through
the rainforest. It has also granteda
licence to the state-run oil
ATE} company, Petrobras, to carry
out explorations for offshore
oil, 500 km away fromthe mouth of
the Amazon River.
Inthe fight against the climate cri-
sis, protecting the Amazon is crucial.
The forest contains 71.5 billion tonnes
of carbon, orroughly double the global
carbon dioxide emissions for 2022. In
recent years, some studies have
argued thatthe Amazon has becomea
source of carbon emissions due to
human actions, like farm fires.
A2022 study, publishedin Nature,
revealed that the Amazon has become
slower at recovering from long
droughts and is nearing its tipping
point. Beyond that point, it would
transform from a lush, green forest
into a drier savanna, releasing a large
amount of stored carbon and further
exacerbating global warming. ENS
